synopsis: Across the booklet, nuisance alarms undermine trust and can lead operators to ignore, override or disable proximity-warning systems, making nuisance rate a safety objective rather than merely a comfort issue [f3306, f7000]. In the NIOSH haul-truck study, drivers found continuous audible warnings annoying because most did not signify danger, and researchers found the warning disabled after shifts; however, the Morenci radar trial reported occasional false alarms that were not frequent enough to cause the system to be ignored [f3280, f3281, f7001]. Automatic braking does not remove this human-factors risk: operators may carry warning-ignore habits into their first automatic stops, while overly conservative triggers can introduce unnecessary braking, fatigue and intervention-created hazards [f1169, f6569]. ISO 21815-3 flags false-positive-induced alarm fatigue, but the booklet found no direct mining measurements of the probability of ignoring successive warnings or longitudinal physiological studies [f2427, f3304, f3305]. On-road evidence is mixed and should remain distinguished from mining evidence: one finding linked an 18% false-alarm rate to drivers ignoring FCW (12%) or giving up on it (11%), whereas a 2025 study found no “cry wolf” effect at 33% false alarms, despite unnecessary braking [f11680, f11682]. Validation therefore needs to address habituation, warning meaning, reaction time, predictable escalation and restart, alongside tuning unnecessary warnings and braking as safety goals [f2924, f14430].

relations.note: Both identify inherited warning-ignore habits as a risk during transition to automatic braking.
Both attribute false-positive alarm-fatigue warnings to ISO 21815-3.
Glossary repeats the draft standard's warning about false positives.
Both report the haul-truck audible warning being disabled after shifts.
Glossary restates the Caterpillar 793B warning-disablement observation.
Both report researchers finding the audible warning disabled after shifts.
Explains why the warning was annoying: most alarms did not indicate danger.
Both report three-country agreement that alarm burden prompts ignoring, bypassing or switching off.
Both identify missing direct mining measurements of successive-warning ignore probability.
Glossary repeats the documented mining precursors and outcomes of alarm fatigue.
Both identify nuisance alarms as the primary reason deployed proximity systems fail.
Both frame nuisance-rate tuning as a safety goal because operators may ignore or disable systems.
Observed warning disablement supports the risk that fatigue leads operators to disable systems.
Different on-road studies report contrasting behavioral effects; false-alarm percentages alone do not reconcile them.
Occasional false alarms did not cause ignoring, qualifying the categorical switch-off prediction across different systems.
Product tests' behavioral prediction limits support broader validation of habituation and operator responses.
Unnecessary braking's fatigue and hazard consequences justify treating intervention frequency as a safety objective.
